replying_to: Replying to Revisiting transposed convolutions for interpreting raw waveform sound event recognition CNNs by sonification
display_title: Official Review of Paper1517 by Reviewer PJrE

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper reports an analysis of CNN-based audio classification models by sonification of feature activations using transposed convolutions (DeconvNet). The CNN models are trained either by supervised learning or self-supervised learning. The authors delineate the observation of sonification by displaying them and comparing different sonification patterns in all layers and the two training methods. They validated the sonification results by showing the performance degradation when they are subtracted from the original input, and computing the coherence between them in spectrum. The appendix provides the details of model architecture, benchmark evaluation on the datasets, and exemplary proof of time-invariance of the input and corresponding sonification to support the main text.
content.main_review:
This paper shows a lot of interesting observation to help understanding CNN models for audio classification and the effect of training methods (supervised vs self-supervised). I respect the effort of the authors for comprehensive experiments on three datasets with different training settings and investigation of the trained models using the DeconvNet. However, this paper has the following major issues to be accepted. 

First, this paper made no technical contribution. This is a serious drawback as an ICLR submission. They simply applied an old (considering fast advance of deep learning) visualization technique to trained CNN models and briefly describes the observations. Furthermore, the authors unfortunately missed the following works that already used the same method to understand CNN models for audio classification. 

- Auralisation of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks: Listening to Learned Features, Keunwoo Choi, Jeonghee Kim, György Fazekas, Mark Sandler, ISMIR LBD, 2015

- Explaining Deep Convolutional Neural Networks on Music Classification, Keunwoo Choi, George Fazekas, Mark Sandler, Arxiv, 2016 (the extended version of the ISMIR LBD paper)

This previous work used the same DeconvNet to auralize the feature activation for CNN trained to classify music genre. Although they used spectrogram as input and music data, the overall idea is the same. They used the term "auralization" instead of sonification. This submitted paper definitely more observations, for example, comparing supervised learning to self-supervised learning and validation of sonification. However, the core idea was already tried long before. 

Second, the validation experiments are also quite plain. Considering the nature of deconvolution, it would be hard to obtain a good quality of reconstructed sonification from deeper layers (they have more paths going through more layers). Therefore, the coherence between the original input and the corresponding sonification are supposed to be lower for deeper layers. The authors might ignore this issue. 

Third, the analysis is not convincing. The observations of sonification are described in a terse manner in session 3.3. I could not find any insight particularly in deeper layers. In addition, when I listened to the audio examples in the footnote link, the sonification examples were not straightforward to understand. Many of audio examples are very noisy and mostly contain high-frequency content (to my ears).   

In addition to the major issues, I have the following questions.

- What is the purpose of Section 4.3? The content is not related to sonification. 

- Most sonification examples contain high-frequency content. I think a regularization or smoothing method in the waveform level might be necessary to suppress the trend. Unlike images, small discontinuity in audio waveforms can cause annoying high-frequency noise. 

- It is unusual to use two entires pages of the main text for displaying images. I understand they are important images to explain the main idea but the style of presentation makes the paper look like a technical report.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper has some interesting observations of CNN-based audio classification using transposed convolution. However, it has critical weakness in technical contributions. Furthermore, the important reference which already attempted a similar analysis is missing. Therefore, I recommend strong reject.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1517 by Reviewer PJrE
display_title: Official Comment addressing Reviewer PJrE's concerns (Comment 1)

content.title: Official Comment addressing Reviewer PJrE's concerns (Comment 1)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for taking the time to review our paper. We would like to address your concerns:

## Major Issue 1
> First, this paper made no technical contribution. This is a serious drawback as an ICLR submission. They simply applied an old (considering fast advance of deep learning) visualization technique to trained CNN models and briefly describes the observations. 

We agree that Deconvnets themselves have been around for a long while, but at the same time, we argue that our contributions include evaluating them in a recent context on raw waveform modelling task that compares two different training paradigms, and providing empirical analysis to support/evaluate those claims using signal processing concepts (Section 4.2 in this work). Although several front-ends for modelling raw waveform signals have been recently proposed, directly consuming raw audio signals is still very much a task of great interest, more so in the (contrastive) self-supervised audio learning space, where prominent recent methods [3-5] directly ingest raw signals without using specific front-ends. We think that evaluation of feature representations learned by these paradigms, using methods old or new, are still of significance and contribution.

---

> Furthermore, the authors unfortunately missed the following works that already used the same method to understand CNN models for audio classification. 

> [1] Auralisation of Deep Convolutional Neural Networks: Listening to Learned Features, Keunwoo Choi, Jeonghee Kim, György Fazekas, Mark Sandler, ISMIR LBD, 2015

> [2] Explaining Deep Convolutional Neural Networks on Music Classification, Keunwoo Choi, George Fazekas, Mark Sandler, Arxiv, 2016 (the extended version of the ISMIR LBD paper)

> However, the core idea was already tried long before.

Missing the above-mentioned work(s) is unfortunate and an oversight. However, there are several differences between [1-2] and the proposed work, and we would like to draw attention to them:

1. As pointed out by the reviewer, [1, 2] apply deconvolution to 2D-CNNs that are trained on spectrogram inputs. We model raw waveform signals directly, and our inversion process goes back into raw waveform space directly, whereas [1,2] recover a discernible audio signal using inverse STFT from the input spectrogram.
2. As pointed out by the reviewer, we provide more observations and compare self-supervised and supervised representations, whereas [1, 2] only cover supervised learning.
3. The dataset utilized by [1, 2] is derived from only 8000 unique songs across 4 classes. This is not a demerit of [1,2], but simply that proposed work is conducted on much larger datasets with a significantly larger ontology of classes. As a result, our representations are more involved and better representative of current trends in audio classification.
4. [1, 2] never justify/demonstrate how the "auralizations" they obtained correspond to elements in the input that are crucial for audio recognition, unlike the proposed work. We understand that Deconvnets, by their very nature, will highlight essential maximally activating substructures in the input, but the onus to verify/evaluate it still rests on the end-user.
5. [1, 2] do not demonstrate how coherence of the interpreted signal varies on a layer-by-layer basis, unlike the proposed work. As correctly pointed out by the reviewer, with increasing depth the coherence will, naturally, decrease (which we confirm in Fig 6), but as we demonstrate, the actual trend of coherence is more nuanced.
6. In [1, 2], the comparison of the "auralized" signals with the input signals is limited. [2] does compare the layerwise correlation of variations of key, chord, and instrument (Fig 10), but to the best of our understanding, no comparisons are made between the input and corresponding interpretations.

We thank the reviewer for bringing [1, 2] to our attention (which is certainly our, the authors, responsibility), and would be happy to cite them and mention how the proposed work fares in comparison. But given the differences, despite using the same core concept, we believe that the proposed paper is sufficiently different in execution and insights revealed.

---

(Continued in comments)

### References
[3] Schneider, S., Baevski, A., Collobert, R., & Auli, M. (2019). wav2vec: Unsupervised Pre-Training for Speech Recognition. In Interspeech 2019 (pp. 3465–3469).

[4] Oord, A. van den, Li, Y., & Vinyals, O. (2018). Representation Learning with Contrastive Predictive Coding. ArXiv Preprint ArXiv:1807.03748.

[5] Baevski, A., Zhou, Y., Mohamed, A., & Auli, M. (2020). wav2vec 2.0: A Framework for Self-Supervised Learning of Speech Representations. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (Vol. 33, pp. 12449–12460).

replying_to: Replying to Official Comment addressing Reviewer PJrE's concerns (Comment 1)
display_title: Official Comment addressing Reviewer PJrE's concerns (Comment 2)

content.title: Official Comment addressing Reviewer PJrE's concerns (Comment 2)
content.comment:
## Major Issue 2
> Considering the nature of deconvolution, it would be hard to obtain a good quality of reconstructed sonification from deeper layers (they have more paths going through more layers). Therefore, the coherence between the original input and the corresponding sonification are supposed to be lower for deeper layers. The authors might ignore this issue.

We completely agree with the reviewer, that the coherence between the original input and the corr. sonification is indeed expected to be lower for deeper layers. But by how much? Has that ever been quantified? And is it the same for self-supervised and supervised representations? We have attempted to quantify it and answer these questions and Fig 6 shows that there are remarkable differences in the coherence of the two training paradigms.

---

## Major Issue 3
> I could not find any insight particularly in deeper layers.

Comparing the audio samples of the supervised and the self-supervised models, at the very least, draws one insightful parallel between the representations of the two paradigms: contrastive model result in more discernible sonifications, whereas supervised learning does not. **But, we will improve the observations made in Sec 3.3**

>  In addition, when I listened to the audio examples in the footnote link, the sonification examples were not straightforward to understand. 
Many of the audio examples are very noisy and mostly contain high-frequency content (to my ears)

We would respectfully like to ask if you listened to both the supervised and the contrastive sonifications. Sonifications for the supervised models are indeed mostly noisy and no clear acoustic events are discernible, esp for the deeper layers, but that's not the case for the contrastive model at all. 

We do agree that there is a fair share of noise in the sonifications, but the AudioSet dataset itself has a lot of background noise. 
**We will pick selected non-noisy samples and their corresponding sonifications and update/augment the audio dashboard, making it concise and simple**, something also requested by another reviewer. Do you believe that will aid the paper?

---

## Addressing Minor Points

> What is the purpose of Section 4.3? The content is not related to sonification.

We agree. We added this as an affirmation that the deeper layers are indeed aiding recognition performance. Do you want us to move Sec 4.3?

> Most sonification examples contain high-frequency content. I think a regularization or smoothing method in the waveform level might be necessary to suppress the trend. Unlike images, small discontinuity in audio waveforms can cause annoying high-frequency noise.

We agree with the reviewer regarding discontinuities in audio waveforms and high-frequency noise. Discontinuities are also expected given the nature of max-unpooling operation that basically inserts maximum values at correct indices, leaving others zero. This is certainly one of the drawbacks of this approach, and we will include this in the revised version of the paper. However, we would like to reiterate the points we made in Major Issue 3 in response. **Kindly give us an opportunity to simplify the audio dashboard.**

> It is unusual to use two entire pages of the main text for displaying images. I understand they are important images to explain the main idea but the style of presentation makes the paper look like a technical report.

Another reviewer (D7LC) have also pointed this out, along with a possible solution. We would like to know your suggestions on how it can be improved and find a common ground.

---

### Closing comments
> I respect the effort of the authors for comprehensive experiments on three datasets with different training settings and investigation of the trained models using the DeconvNet

We appreciate that. Thank you, Reviewer PJrE. 

Regarding the novelty of the proposed work, contributions and other comments, we have made our case the best we could. We agree that the method of interpretation (DeconvNets) in itself is not novel, but

1. The application to evaluating self-supervised representations in raw waveform CNNs by interpreting them directly in the input signal space and comparing them with supervised representations is new.
2. Quantifying how coherence between input and sonified signals varies for supervised and self-supervised representations is also a respectable technical contribution, which none of the existing works has made, irrespective of how obvious and trivial it may seem.

So we respectfully disagree with the notion that we simply applied DeconvNets: we believe that's an oversimplification and undermines quite a bit of exploratory and empirical analysis done that is different from prior works, including [1,2]. 

We're hopeful the reviewer will see our efforts to improve the quality of the manuscript, as well as the differences we have highlighted with previous works. We're open to any other suggestions made by them for the same.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The manuscript covers an interesting topic, mapping feature representations back into the discrete-time input signal space for a better interpretation as intelligible acoustic events.
the authors have proposed to use sonification as a method to interpret intermediate feature representations of
sound event recognition convolutional neural networks (CNNs) trained on raw waveforms. Utilizing the sonification methods, the CNN representation of the features is mapped back into the discrete-time input signal domain, highlighting substructures in the input that maximally activate a feature map as intelligible acoustic events. 
The authors claim that by using sonification it is possible to compare supervised and self-supervised feature hierarchies and show how the interpretability of SER models.
content.main_review:
interpretability of the intermediate CNN features in the SER applications is a useful tool that could improve the state-of-the-art models significantly if the extracted information is fed back to the network to improve the training process or the evaluation process during the test. 
The authors in this manuscript have made the following claims: 

1- revisiting transposed convolutions (a.k.a. deconvolutions) for interpreting intermediate feature representations of raw-waveform based 1D-CNNs for sound event recognition (SER) by sonification, highlighting maximally activating substructures as intelligible
acoustic events.
** This claim is supported in the manuscript. 
2- Using sonifications, to compare and contrast supervised and self-supervised feature representations in the audio signal input space
** I can't find enough supporting material for this claim. 
** The authors could conduct a supervised and self-supervised feature representations training procedure utilizing the proposed method, then compare the final feature representation on unseen data and perform some evaluation metrics to support this claim. 
** The authors have presented the evaluation results in Figures 6-8, however, the message is not conveyed properly nor clearly. 
3- Demonstrating how sonifications facilitate the visualization and spectral inspection of SER models, working synergistically with signal processing techniques.
** There is not enough supporting material for this claim. 

I highly recommend to the authors conduct more comprehensive experiments and analyses to assess how this approach could provide improvement compared to a regular embedding learning mechanism. 
How could this work be compared to some of the existing SER embedding networks such as L3 network?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1517 by Reviewer 7P67

content.title: Official Comment addressing Reviewer 7P67's concerns
content.comment:
Thank you for taking the time to review our paper. We have the following comments:

## ISSUE: Insufficient support for claim #2
> 2- Using sonifications, to compare and contrast supervised and self-supervised feature representations in the audio signal input space ** I can't find enough supporting material for this claim. *

> The authors could conduct a supervised and self-supervised feature representations training procedure utilizing the proposed method, then compare the final feature representation on unseen data and perform some evaluation metrics to support this claim.
 
We believe there has been some misunderstanding in either the way we have conveyed the objective of the work/set the scope of the work or the way the reviewer has interpreted it. We attempt to clarify this:

1. We have done exactly that; we conducted supervised and self-supervised training and compared final feature representations empirically by mapping intermediate representations back into the audio input space and listening to them as well as experimentally/numerically quantifying how sonifications and the input audio signal compare to each other.
2. We also provide comprehensive experimentation on 3 benchmark datasets (which was commended by another reviewer), establishing baseline recognition performance.
3. Our primary objective is not benchmarking recognition performance (as we have stated), but rather interpretations of simple and straightforward CNN baselines by mapping representations back into the audio input space.
4. The proposed method is not meant for training SER models at all, nor is it claimed to improve performance by doing that.
 
> The authors have presented the evaluation results in Figures 6-8, however, the message is not conveyed properly nor clearly

We would appreciate it if the reviewer can describe how we can make the message proper and clear. That will aid in improving the quality of the paper. Also, **we do not have a Figure 8** in our paper, can you please tell us which figure you're referring to?

---

## ISSUE: Insufficient support for claim #3
> Demonstrating how sonifications facilitate the visualization and spectral inspection of SER models, working synergistically with signal processing techniques. **There is not enough supporting material for this claim**

We devote an entire section (Sec 4.2) that shows how sonifications worked with signal processing techniques (Spectral Coherence) to facilitate inspection of the proposed self-supervised and supervised baselines. 

**However, we do realize and understand your concern about how broad this objective statement seems. We will correct the scope of this statement, limiting it to exactly how we have used Spectral Coherence in our work, putting it in the correct context.** Does that seem right to you?

---

## ISSUE: How this approach provide improvement compared to a regular embedding learning mechanism?

> I highly recommend to the authors conduct more comprehensive experiments and analyses to assess how this approach could provide improvement compared to a regular embedding learning mechanism. How could this work be compared to some of the existing SER embedding networks such as L3 network?

Again, we believe either we misconveyed the scope of our work, or the reviewer misinterpreted it. Let us clarify:

We do not seek to provide an improvement over existing embedding learning mechanisms or SER methods. As clearly stated in **Sec 3.1** and **A.1** of the paper, we do not propose a new state-of-the-art method, nor do we draw a comparison as to how better our approach is at SER than existing approaches. We have provided ample performance comparisons with some recent and prominent baseline in the literature on multiple benchmarks (Tables **A.3-A.6**) to ascertain that our feature encoder is fit for analysis. **We understand how comparison with another architecture might facilitate evaluation, but that will defeat the objective of the paper.**

The objective of the paper is to interpret self-supervised and supervised raw waveform SER CNNs using transposed convolutions (DeconvNets) and use signal processing techniques to compare sonifications and input signals to aid interpretability. So we firmly believe this issue is unfortunately beyond the scope of the proposed work.

---

**We would be happy to clear any other doubts of the reviewer and aid them in understanding our work to the best of our abilities. We would be happy to provide experiments on any other datasets that the reviewer expects to see evaluated on**. Currently, it seems like they're asking us to do things that we believe are out of the scope of the paper, such as comparing with L3 architecture. We believe they're referring to L3-Net from [1], which is an architecture for image and audio multimodal recognition.

---

**References**

[1] Arandjelovic, Relja, and Andrew Zisserman. "Look, listen and learn." Proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision. 2017.

replying_to: Replying to Revisiting transposed convolutions for interpreting raw waveform sound event recognition CNNs by sonification
display_title: Official Review of Paper1517 by Reviewer D7LC

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces the idea of sonification, an approach to interpret hidden representation learned by a CNN-based model taking the raw waveform as input. This approach is applied to the Sound Event Detection task. The sonification algorithm is first presented and then applied to two training cases: contrastive and supervised traning. The resulting sonification are then presented and discussed. Several studies are then presented, showing that sonification signals are an important sub-structure of the input signal, analysing the two training approaches and analyzing the importance of the layers.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- The main idea of the paper, sonification, is very appealing and signiifcant: interpretability of audio-based neural networks is an open question and the proposed approach is a solid avenue of research for this issue. 

Weaknesses:
- The paper is very strangly structured, making it very hard to understand. Here are my main concerns:
    - Section 3.1 especially is very hard to undersand, as nothing is really explained. It simply provide references that the reader must know in order to understand the paper. I think this is quite bad, a paper should be self-contained as much as possible. Section 3.1 should be 1-2 pages long and explain clearly every step. 
    - Section 3.2 is also missing definition, for instance "s" is not defined at the beginning. The algorithm is not easy to grasp, a figure would have help a lot. Also, it's still unclear to me what the loss function is to train the Transposed Convolution layers for the sonification.
   - Section 3.3 is impossible to parse. Figure 1 and 2 have way too much information, and very little indication of what these figures are supposed to represent. Trying to follow the third bullet point observations is way harder than it should be, and it's clearly a pain point for the reader. My advice here is to isolate the interesting sonification plots and create a figure for each case, with a clear caption.
   - Section 3.4 has the same problem as 3.3: too much information, and I don't know what I am looking at.
   - Some useful information are in the appendix, i suggest that the two pages figures should be trimmed and some info about the architecture and the experimental setup should be brought in the main paper.

Overall, these issues about clarity make the proposed visualisation technique hard to evaluate. The audio examples provided are also quite confusing, as the input is very noisy, hence it's not clear what the sonifiaction signal means. I think selecting better examples would help, specially the ones mentionned in Section 3.3, for instance i would like to listen to the house/trap music example.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The goal of the paper is very noble, interpretability of neural networks is an important area, specially in audio-based model. The proposed approach of sonification is quite novel and significant, and overall a good step towards intepretable audio model. However, the paper is very hard to read and makes the proposed approach hard to understand and to evaluate.

I was very excited by this paper when i read the abstract, but in the current form i cannot recommend acceptance. I will be happy to increase my score if the authors improve the clarity of the paper.

content.title: Official Comment addressing Reviewer D7LC's concerns
content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing our work. We'd first like to address the major concerns regarding clarity of the paper raised by the reviewer, followed by misc comments.

## Critical Concern #1: Regarding Sec 3.1 and important information in the appendix
> Section 3.1 especially is very hard to undersand, as nothing is really explained. It simply provide references that the reader must know in order to understand the paper. I think this is quite bad, a paper should be self-contained as mcu has possible. Section 3.1 should be 1-2 pages long and explain clearly every step.

> Some useful information are in the appendix, i suggest that the two pages figures should be trimmed and some info about the architecture and the experimental setup should be brought in the main paper

We believe both of these issues can be addressed by moving information from the appendix that concerns the architecture and other design choices to the main section, and removing the two pages of figures (Fig 1 and 2) and restricting to visualizations of only samples in spotlight, as discussed in Observations in Sec 3.3. 

Our reasoning behind not including training benchmarks and results in the main section were that we didn't want to overly emphasize the benchmark and performance aspects of the paper, as that was never our primary objective nor our primary concern. We would be happy to include more information about the CNN12 feature encoder, the contrastive loss function in the main paper! 

---

## Critical Concern #2: Simplifying the sonification process
> Section 3.2 is also missing definition, for instance "s" is not defined at the beginning. The algorithm is not easy to grasp, a figure would have helped a lot.

We can certainly create a figure that depicts the sonification process in more detail. Our reasoning behind leaving this out was that the DeconvNet process for interpreting is quite well known. But we understand your concerns regarding how self-contained the paper is. We will add this figure to the revised version of the paper.

> Also, it's still unclear to me what the loss function is to train the Transposed Convolution layers for the sonification

The transposed convolution layers are not trained separately; they share weights with the corresponding convolution layer in the feature encoder, and the process is non-parametric in the sense that no optimization of transposed convolution layers is required. We will be more clear about that in the revised paper.
 
---

## Critical Concern #3
> Section 3.4 has the same problem as 3.3: too much information, and i don't know what i am looking at.

We will definitely address that.

---

## Critical Concern #4: Audio Samples

> The audio examples provided are also quite confusing, as the input is very noisy, hence it's not clear what the sonifiaction signal means. I think selecting better examples would help, specially the ones mentionned in Section 3.3, for instance i would like to listen to the house/trap music example.

This issue has also been raised by other reviewers (which we have attempted to address in the comments). Given that the AudioSet dataset is taken from real-world video clips, there is a lot of background and static noise in a lot of the audio clips. 

We will create an additional audio dashboard with only selective sonification examples, separately for the contrastive and supervised representations, especially the ones in Section 3.3. We'll also try to include these samples in the paper's official code repository.

---

## *QUESTION* 

Do you believe the steps mentioned above would be sufficient to address your concerns? Please let us know. 

---

### Misc comments
> The main idea of the paper, sonification, is very appealing and signiifcant: interpretability of audio-based neural networks is an open question and the proposed approach is a solid avenue of research for this issue

> I was very excited by this paper when i read the abstract, but in the current form i cannot recommend acceptance. I will be happy to increase my score if the authors improve the clarity of the paper.

We really appreciate that, thank you Reviewer D7LC. We are glad to hear that the abstract excited you! We will address your concerns soon and come back with an improved manuscript.

content.title: Response to authors' rebuttal
content.comment:
First I'd like to thank the authors for the very thorough rebuttal and for updating the paper. I think the paper looks better now, and adresses some of my concerns about clarity. Unfortunately, there are still issues with the paper:
- In terms of clarity, Section 3 is better but it's still confusing: Section 3.1 presents the experimental setup for the proposed approach, which is presented in later in Section 3.2. It even starts with the sentence " To test the proposed method ..." when the approach haven't been proposed yet. I think switching 3.1 and 3.2 would help.
- The similarity with (Choi et al., 2015,2016) is a bit concerning in terms of novelty, as pointed out by Reviewer PJrE. The authors provided a discussion about it, but it still does limit the novelty of the paper. My suggestion for the authors is to apply their approach on speech data. I am convinced the sonification will be very interesting and will help differentiate the paper from Choi et al.
- The paper claims to be an extension of (Zeiler & Fergus, 2014), but the main acheivement of the 2014 paper was to provide significant insights about what CNNs learned in the different layers. In the submitted paper, the insights presented are very limited and i don't think they change the way we undertand CNNs using raw audio. Maybe it's due to the different type of audio used, using speech only could help gaining more signifiant insights.
- As Reviewer 7P67 suggested, a comparison with a known method would be useful to assess the usefulness of the proposed approach.

To conclude, i enjoyed the paper but it's unfortunately it has too many issues to be accepted. Hence I will keep my score as it is. I strongly encourage the authors to keep pursuing this line of research.

content.title: Official comment addressing Reviewer r61T's concerns
content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing our paper. We would like to make the following comments:

---

> This paper presents an interesting idea on how to visualize and interpret intermedia representations of SER CNNs, providing visualization, experiments/analysis on its impacts for a couple of downstream tasks, with different training approaches. Overall this paper is clear written, and it provides some insights for better understanding representations for SER.

We thank the reviewer for their general comments regarding the proposed work providing useful insights that improve understanding of SER representations. That was our primary objective in undertaking this study.

---

> Overall, I find methodologies presented in this paper relatively straightforward with limited novelty.

We agree, DeconvNets are not new, and have certainly been used for interpreting audio CNNs before (as pointed out by Reviewer PJrE).  But the proposed work does address several aspects of interpretability of audio CNNs that haven't been evaluated before.

1. The application to evaluating supervised and self-supervised representations in raw waveform CNNs in the input space is novel.
2. Quantifying how coherence between input and sonified signals varies for supervised and self-supervised representations is also a new, technical contribution.

Our paper indeed focuses solely on interpretability with very few benchmarks and datasets evaluated. But we believe that irrespective of the simplicity of the approach, a thorough evaluation of an old technique if it leads to important and new insights (which the reviewer themselves pointed out), is a worthy objective. 

---

>  It may better fit speech/audio-focused forums

We understand that assessment. But we also want to know the reviewer's opinion on the ways in which the evaluation, in the context of the given work, is insufficient, and how can it be improved.

We submitted the paper to ICLR because representation learning is a core topic of the conference, and as per the mission statement, new, relevant, impactful, and insightful knowledge is valued, so we do not believe that the submission is out of scope.

---

> One questions: For "deep supervised layers learn the presence of more abstract concepts" at the end of Sec 3.3, what does "abstract concepts" refer to?

By abstract concepts, we simply mean that the sonifications corresponding to the deeper supervised layers do not contain intelligible acoustic elements, despite their significant contribution to recognition performance and the wide-variety of maximally activating inputs. We will rephrase this statement in the revised version of the paper and make it clear.

content.title: Paper revision overview and response to all reviewers
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their feedback and suggestions. We found them very useful to improve the paper and better present the observations we made in the paper as well as in the accompanying audio dashboard. We summarize the changes made to the paper in response to points raised by reviewers:

## Major Changes

---

### 1. Add missing references, compare them with proposed work (Reviewer PJrE)

- We have added the missing references as pointed out by Reviewer PJrE. Related Works section now clearly mentions how they have used transposed convolutions for music classification for spectrogram input and also the differences between them and the proposed work. We are tremendously thankful to Reviewer PJrE for bringing this to our attention.

---

### 2. Changes in Figures, Sec 3 (Reviewer D7LC and PJrE)

1. **Replacing the 2 large full-page figures and replacing them with smaller, select sonification plots**: In line with the recommendation from Reviewer's D7LC and PJrE, the large figures have been replaced by 3 smaller ones that consist of select sonifications that support the observations made directly.

2. **Replacing the 2 large training time feature evolution figures with a single figure**: In line with the recommendation from Reviewer D7LC, removed the 2 large figures from 3.4 with a single figure that consists of select contrastive feature maps.

---

### 3. Improving Observations in Section 3.3 and 3.4 (Reviewer D7LC and PJrE)

- Observations in Sec 3.3 and Sec 3.4 made easier to read. 
- Also reduced how terse Observations in Section 3.3 were.

---

### 4. Select Audio Samples, Simplying the Audio Dashboard (Reviewer D7LC and PJrE)

1. **Picking select input samples and sonifications**: Remove noisy samples and restrict dashboards to select audio samples, making them easier to listen to and evaluate. Addressing both Reviewer D7LC and PJrE's issues. 
2. **Separating the audio dashboards for Supervised and Contrastive models, and simplifying them**: The previous dashboard had the same landing page for sonifications of both models. In particular, supervised sonifications have more high-frequency noise, and we suspected this was causing confusion. Now they're cleaner, with much fewer samples, and well separated. Addressing both Reviewer D7LC and PJrE's issues
3. **Attaching selected samples as supplementary material**: We have also added a zip-file containing all sonifications with a README that contains info on how to find the precise samples we mention in the paper. (As specifically requested by Reviewer D7LC)

---

### 5. Better explanation of the Sonification Process, Sec 3.2 (Reviewer D7LC)
1. **Improved readability of Sec 3.2** describing the sonification process, added missing definitions. 
2. Clearly mention how transposed convolutions share weights with the conv layers and require no additional training. 
3. **Add Pseudocode for the sonification process**: Instead of adding a figure (we felt that the paper already has a lot of figures), we added pseudocode in the appendix describing the sonification process in Pythonic syntax.

---

### 6. Adding information about the architecture and training setup to Sec 3.1 (Reviewer D7LC)
As per Reviewer D7LC's recommendation, after replacing the large figures, we have moved some essential information about the neural architecture, training and evaluation setup to the main paper in Sec 3.1

---

### 7. Adding clarifying statement about Coherence (Reviewer PJrE)
- Reviewer PJrE raised the concern (and we paraphrase) that "given the nature of deconvolution, coherence is expected to decrease with layer depth due to difficulty reconstructing". 
- We reverted by saying that this is expected yes, but quantifying it and how quantifying it helped highlight a difference between supervised and self-supervised representations makes this of sufficient significance.
- This is now overtly stated in Sec 4.2.

---

### 8. Moving layerwise performance evaluation for FSD50K and Speech Commands v2 (Reviewer PJrE)
- The section itself has been moved to appendix
- The figure has been kept in the main paper. Motivation for doing the experiment has been added to the figure caption: when we first observed sonifications for the supervised and contrastive models, the significantly lower activity in the deep supervised layers made us sceptical about them.

---

### 9. Regarding High-Frequency noise in sonifications from deeper Supervised layers (Reviewer PJrE)
- addressed this in the paper. listed possible reasons
- since these are not as prominent in the self-supervised representations, concluded that it's possible this is most likely a qualitative effect of what the supervised representations learn, and requires further investigation to be sure.

---

**Minor changes and closing comments in continued thread..**

replying_to: Replying to Paper revision overview and response to all reviewers

content.title: (continued)
content.comment:
## Minor changes

---

**1. Reducing the scope of statement 3 (Reviewer 7P67)**
We have reduced the scope of the statement "Demonstrating how sonifications facilitate the visualization and spectral inspection of SER models, working synergistically with signal processing techniques", and now limited it precisely to our usage of Spectral Coherence.

**2. Clarification of doubt by Reviewer r61T**
- elaborated what we meant by "abstract concepts" at the end of Sec 3.3

**3. Improving readability of all figures**

---

## Closing Comments

Overall, we did our best to thoroughly address all pain points raised by the reviewers. We hope that these changes, and our comments, will be taken into consideration. 

We agree that the approach is "simple" and has been used in a related domain, but we have pointed out several differences as well as the added evaluation that makes this work different from the previous works. 

All the reviewers point out that the work is interesting and has some interesting observations, but 3/4 comment that the evaluation itself is "plain" and "too simple". We simply ask: but is the evaluation incorrect? **(All reviewers have rated the work a 3 on the correctness scale, so we believe there is agreement that to a large extent, the evaluation is correct.)** Are the observations made obvious/well known and no different than those made in previous work? Has anyone else quantified the similarity between audio interpretations and corresponding inputs and demonstrated differences between supervised and self-supervised representations, using a similar approach, and is our approach for doing so valid/invalid? We would have appreciated feedback on these aspects of the paper!
